# It was great to be back at Stanford University, with the Stanford Applied Cyber group a few weeks ago. | Vineet Edupuganti · LinkedIn · 2025-12-18

**Vineet Edupuganti**: Co-Founder and CEO at Cogent Security with 1 year of total professional experience. Previous roles include Head of Multi Product Platform Division at Abnormal AI. Based in San Francisco, California, United States [US].

---

It was great to be back at Stanford University, with the [Stanford Applied Cyber](https://linkedin.com/company/applied-cyber) group a few weeks ago.

I was invited back to my alma mater to speak about my journey through cybersecurity to founding [Cogent Security](https://linkedin.com/company/cogentsecurity) - from sitting in their chairs, to joining Abnormal AI as an early employee, to now building my own company in the space.

Spending time with students who are truly passionate about cybersecurity is always energizing, and it’s great to see the depth of talent in the next generation.

Thanks for having me [Ashley Dai](https://linkedin.com/in/ashleydai), and for helping build this incredible community of future cyber leaders.

It was an honor to join my longtime mentor Evan Reiser at Black Hat for a conversation hosted by Abnormal AI, with expert moderation by Corinne Marie Riley from Greylock Partners. Evan has been the most influential leader in my career. I had the privilege of learning directly under him for years, and much of how I think about modern company building and cybersecurity traces back to that experience. We covered a wide range of topics, from the rapidly evolving threat landscape to how AI-native companies like Abnormal AI and Cogent Security are shaping the future of defense. Some takeaways: - The attack surface is expanding and threats are accelerating daily - Autonomous defense is inevitable, but adoption depends on efficacy and user experience - AI-native DNA will separate the winners from the laggards - When choosing a role, optimize for company potential and talent density. With intensity, follow-through, and constant learning, you can compress decades of growth into just a few years Full discussion linked in the comments.

# Why end-to-end problems matter in product management

https://www.linkedin.com/in/vineetedupuganti

Vineet Edupuganti

Co-founder & CEO @ Cogent Security | Ex-Abnormal AI

9mo

- Report this post

In my experiences as a product leader at Abnormal AI and now as a co-founder at Cogent Security, I’ve shipped a number of products and advised dozens of Product Managers doing the same across leading tech companies. One mistake I see over and over: solving point problems instead of end-to-end problems. For example: in cybersecurity and engineering, you can perfectly prioritize which alerts/bugs to fix first, but if no one knows who’s responsible for fixing them, nothing actually gets done. The process only works when every step connects. Good product management means meeting customers where they are, solving an end-to-end problem, and guiding them toward a desired future state. But what about the advice to “do one thing really well”? There’s truth to it, but that one thing needs to be more than just an individual feature. It needs to be a complete and well thought out workflow, even if it spans multiple layers. Fortunately, in the age of AI, the ROI calculus around software development has also changed. # From Hoop Dreams to Science Stardom

Mar 28, 2017

By Vineet Edupuganti, senior at Oregon Episcopal School and Regeneron Science Talent Search 2017 finalist

If you had told me in 2005 that I would end up falling in love with science, I would have laughed and called you crazy. You see, as a five-year-old — with infinite experience and wisdom under my belt — I was certain that I was going to be a professional basketball player. To me, that job would be the best of all worlds, allowing me to explore my newfound love of numbers by analyzing my statistics, all while playing my favorite sport.

In case you were wondering, that dream didn’t take long to fizzle out. After a few years, I realized that being the tallest kid in my grade equated to nothing more than operating as an undersized point guard, and my interests slowly turned to other areas like history, geography and eventually, science.
